pm_exper_user_3559_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.question: How can I stop letting fear of failure hold me back from trying new things?
pm_exper_user_3559_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.all_options:
(a) Past mistakes can stick in your mind, but they don’t have to be the script for what comes next. See every new challenge as an experiment—if it doesn’t work out, take what you learned and move on without taking it as a personal verdict.
(b) That unfinished degree from the four-year school might still haunt you, but it doesn’t erase all the experience you’ve stacked since then. See each new thing as a test roast—low stakes, meant for learning—so you can focus on refining rather than proving yourself in one go.
(c) Dropping out of the four-year program before community college might feel like a shadow, but you’ve been running the floor and curating the vibe in your coffee shop long enough to know you can adapt. Think of trying something new like discovering a fresh Oakland hip‑hop artist—sometimes the raw, early tracks are the best part of the journey.
(d) Remember that dropping out of that four-year program before transferring to community college doesn’t define the skills and grit you’ve built since. Treat new challenges like pulling a first shot of espresso—if it’s not perfect, you adjust and try again without assuming the machine’s broken.

[] My old coworker’s been stressing about whether to apply for a leadership role at her new job. She keeps saying she’s worried about getting in over her head and not living up to expectations. It’s weird because she’s great at what she does, but she says it reminds her of the last time she took a big leap and it didn’t work out—like when she left that university program early before switching to community college. How can I help her build confidence about taking this step without just saying 'you’ll be fine'?
[] One way to help her build confidence is to focus on reframing what success would look like for her in this leadership role. Instead of treating it as an all-or-nothing pass/fail situation, encourage her to see it as an opportunity to grow her skills, even if the path has a few bumps along the way.

You could help her list out times she’s already stepped up in smaller ways—projects she led, decisions she made under pressure—and how she handled them well. Tangible reminders of past wins can counter the brain’s tendency to fixate on the one time things didn’t go as planned.

It might also help to break the leap into smaller, less intimidating steps. For example, she could talk to someone already in a similar role there to learn what the day-to-day reality is, or even ask her manager if there’s a way to test some of those responsibilities before officially applying.

Finally, validate that her caution comes from caring about doing a good job—remind her that this thoughtful approach is actually an asset in leadership. By shifting the narrative from 'what if I fail' to 'how can I best prepare,' she’s more likely to see herself as capable and ready for the challenge.

Instead of refreshing every few months, you could introduce small tweaks weekly, or even daily rotations in certain areas. That way, you move the novelty stimulus into fresh territory while the rest of your routine holds steady.

Think of it like rotating crops in a field: you keep the land (your core routine) the same, but you grow different plants on it more often so it doesn't wear out.

[] Why do some people get more drained than inspired by little side projects?
[] It can happen for a mix of psychological, emotional, and even environmental reasons — and it's actually not as rare as people think.

One big factor is **cognitive load**. Small creative projects might seem “low effort” from the outside, but they still require mental planning, decision-making, and switching between modes of thinking. If someone’s main job or daily routine already uses their creative bandwidth — say, curating music playlists for a café vibe or finding the perfect way to present a latte — their brain may file extra projects as ‘more work’ rather than ‘fun play’.

There’s also **motivation style** to consider. Some people thrive on variety and novelty (what psychologists sometimes call a high “openness to experience”), while others feel more satisfaction from diving deeply into one or two bigger commitments rather than spreading themselves thin. If you’re in a phase of life where your focus is on doing one thing really well — whether that’s improving at your job, honing a particular skill, or focusing on personal downtime — bite-sized projects can feel like distractions rather than energizers.

Another subtle factor: **context overlap**. If a person’s day job or main activity heavily overlaps with the skills those side projects require, they stop feeling like a refreshing break. For example, if you already work in an artistic, community-focused environment, a personal creative hobby that uses the same muscles can blur with work. That blur can make it harder to feel recharged.

And then there’s the **mental energy vs. reward mismatch**. A small project still needs you to imagine, create, troubleshoot, and finish it — but the ‘reward’ (personal satisfaction, recognition, novelty) might feel too small compared to the energy spent. That makes the experience subtly draining.

Finally, personal rhythms change over time. Maybe a few years ago, small creative tasks felt like a spark; now, you might get that same spark from something totally different — like being out in the city with a camera just capturing candid moments, or letting music run in the background while people-watching.

So it’s not about a lack of creativity — more about where your energy and inspiration tank gets filled. It’s completely natural for that to shift.
